subject: Religionskunskap
title: Hinduism and Buddhism
sourceSummary: The two great religions with roots in India — Hinduism's images of gods, karma and reincarnation, Buddhism's view of suffering and nirvana, holy places and rites, and how they differ from the Abrahamic religions.

questions.prompt: Which statement about gods within Hinduism fits best?
questions.opener: The number of images of gods is large — but many Hindus describe them as parts of something greater.
choices: Within Hinduism people believe in a single god and reject all images of gods
Within Hinduism there are no gods at all
Within Hinduism there are many gods, often described as different sides of the same divine power, brahman
Within Hinduism only Buddha is worshipped
questions.explanation: Hinduism has many gods, for example Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva, Lakshmi and Ganesha, and many Hindus explain them as different expressions of a single divine power called brahman. Rejecting images of gods is instead typical of Judaism and Islam, and Buddha belongs to Buddhism.

questions.opener: The concept is about what actions lead to, not about what you believe in.
choices: The idea that actions have consequences that affect a person's future and coming lives
A holy building in India
The name of Hinduism's holy scripture
A particular fasting period
questions.explanation: Karma means action, and the idea is that both good and bad actions have consequences that affect the life you are born into next. Hinduism's most sacred scriptures are instead called the Vedas, so that option confuses two entirely different concepts.

questions.opener: The word literally means to become flesh again.
choices: That after death you go to a paradise forever
That the soul is born again in a new body after death
That the body is preserved so it can be used again
That you never die if you live rightly
questions.explanation: Reincarnation, or transmigration of the soul, is the idea that the soul is reborn in a new body after death, and the cycle of life and death is called samsara. Belief in an eternal paradise straight after death belongs instead to the Abrahamic religions.

questions.opener: He lived in northern India about 2,500 years ago and left behind a life of wealth.
choices: A god who created the world
A king in China who banned religion
A Hindu god with an elephant head
Siddhartha Gautama, a prince in northern India who, according to Buddhism, attained enlightenment
questions.explanation: According to tradition, Buddha was the prince Siddhartha Gautama, who left his comfortable life to seek the answer to why people suffer, and who attained enlightenment under a fig tree. The word buddha means the awakened one — within Buddhism he is therefore not regarded as a creator god. The god with an elephant head is Ganesha within Hinduism.

questions.opener: It's the goal of the entire Buddhist path.
choices: The name of Buddhism's holy scripture
A large temple building in Nepal
A state in which suffering and the cycle of rebirth cease
The day on which Buddha was born
questions.explanation: According to Buddhism, nirvana is the state in which desires, and thereby suffering, are extinguished, and in which the cycle of rebirth ceases — it is the goal of the Eightfold Path. So it is not a building, a scripture or a festival day.

questions.prompt: What most clearly distinguishes Buddhism from Judaism, Christianity and Islam?
questions.opener: Think about what role a creator god plays in each religion.
choices: Buddhism has no holy texts or buildings
In Buddhism no creator god is at the centre — instead the teaching is about the path away from suffering
Buddhism has no rules at all for how to live
Buddhism arose in the Middle East just like the three others
questions.explanation: The clearest difference is that Buddhism has no creator god at its centre; the focus lies on insight, meditation and the path out of suffering. Buddhism does, however, have both holy texts and temples, and it has clear ethical rules — and it arose in India, not in the Middle East.

questions.prompt: Explain why the river Ganges is a holy place within Hinduism and describe what pilgrims do there.
questions.opener: Think about what water is often used to symbolise in religions, and what Hindus want to achieve.
questions.answer: Within Hinduism the Ganges is regarded as a holy river, and the river is sometimes described as the goddess Ganga. Many Hindus believe that the river can cleanse a person of bad deeds. That's why pilgrims travel to cities along the river, above all Varanasi, to bathe in the water and perform rituals with prayer, lights and flowers. Many also want the ashes of a deceased relative to be scattered in the Ganges, since according to tradition this can help the soul move on in the cycle and closer to liberation, moksha. The fact that the river is used both in the rites of life and at death makes it one of Hinduism's most important holy places.
steps: The Ganges is regarded as holy within Hinduism and is sometimes described as the goddess Ganga.
Many Hindus believe the river's water can cleanse a person of bad deeds.
Pilgrims travel to cities along the river, especially Varanasi, to bathe and perform rituals with prayer, lights and flowers.
The ashes of the deceased are often scattered in the river, since according to tradition this helps the soul move on towards moksha.
Conclusion: the Ganges is holy because it ties together purification, rites and the view of life after death.

questions.prompt: Summarise Hinduism and Buddhism and compare them with the Abrahamic religions.
questions.opener: Take Hinduism first, then Buddhism, and finish with the similarities and differences.
questions.answer: Hinduism: arose in India, the world's oldest of the major religions, no single founder · holy scriptures the Vedas, also the Bhagavad Gita · many gods, e.g. Brahma (the creator), Vishnu (the preserver), Shiva (the destroyer), Ganesha and Lakshmi, often seen as sides of brahman · building temple · karma: actions have consequences · samsara: the cycle of rebirth · moksha: liberation from the cycle, Hinduism's goal · holy places the river Ganges and the city of Varanasi · festival Diwali, the festival of lights · Buddhism: founder Siddhartha Gautama, Buddha, in northern India about 2,500 years ago · no creator god at the centre · four noble truths: suffering exists, it is caused by desire, it can cease, the Eightfold Path leads there · nirvana: the state in which suffering and rebirth cease · meditation is a central practice · monks and nuns live in monasteries · symbol the dharma wheel · Similarities between the two: karma, rebirth and the goal of escaping the cycle · Difference from Judaism, Christianity and Islam: there a single creator god, revelation and a life after death are central, while Hinduism and Buddhism emphasise rebirth and liberation from the cycle.
